newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Hague war crimes trial stalls, lacking witnesses.
newsitem.headline: Hague war crimes trial stalls, lacking witnesses.

text.p: The U.N. trial of Bosnian Serb Dusan "Dusko" Tadic, the first person to face prosecution for alleged war crimes in the former Yugoslavia, was delayed for the second time in two weeks on Wednesday, when defence lawyers ran out of available witnesses.
Presiding judge Gabrielle Kirk McDonald showed uncharacteristic frustration as she adjourned the court until next Wednesday, urging defence council not to delay proceedings.
Defence lawyer Steven Kay, whose team has called just seven witnesses in two weeks, said a second batch would travel from Bosnia to testify in The Hague early next week.
The defence case has repeatedly run into difficulties.
A number of witnesses have withdrawn for fear of being identified, Kay said, while simply transporting them to the Hague-based court has proved complicated.

"We can't just pick up the phone and call witnesses...we have to go through special channels," Kay told Reuters. He said that fellow defence lawyer Michail Wladimiroff was traveling to Bosnia this weekend to coordinate the next round of witnesses.
Tadic, 40, a former cafe owner, denies murdering, torturing and raping Moslems at prison camps in northwest Bosnia during a Serb campaign of ethnic cleansing in 1992.
He says he has never visited the notorious Omarska camp and describing himself as a victim of mistaken identity.

Earlier on Wednesday, two former neighbours of Tadic said the accused was in Banja Luka when Serbs shelled and subsequently evacuated the predominantly Moslem town of Kozarac in northwest Bosnia in late May 1992.

Prosecution witnesses have placed Tadic in his home town of Kozarac when shelling broke out there on May 24, but witness "X", a Croat then living in Banja Luka, said Tadic and his family had been at her house that day.

"X", who has known Tadic for more than 20 years, said the accused had been "highly depressed". "Dusko said he didn't want to put on his uniform because he didn't want to take part in the attack on his neighbours," she said.

A second witness, Serb locksmith Drogolje Balta, said Tadic had stayed at his neighbour's house in Banja Luka until the end of July 1992. He also said Tadic was in Banja Luka at the time of the attack on Kozarac.
Most of the charges against Tadic relate to events between May and the end of August 1992.
The trial, now in its fifth month, has heard from 75 prosecution witnesses.
The U.N. criminal tribunal for the former Yugoslavia has to date indicted 75 suspects -- 54 Serbs, 18 Croats and three Moslems. Tadic is one of seven suspected war criminals in custody in The Hague.
